parties: Mema S.R.L. Società Agricola v Community Plant Variety Office
title: CPVO BoA A014/2020 P - Braeburn 78
text:
CPVO BOARD OF APPEAL PROCEDURAL DECISION DATED 9 NOVEMBER 2022
concerning an objection raised pursuant to Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 2100/94
in Case A014/2020 regarding Community Plant Variety Right Application No 2009/0954
(Variety denomination ‘Braeburn 78’, Species ‘Malus domestica Borkh.)
concerning:
Mema S.R.L. Società Agricola ‘Appellant’ or ‘Party Raising the Objection’
Via Chiesa 54
39018 Terlano (BZ)
Italy
Represented by:
Wuesthoff & Wuesthoff
Patentanwälte PartG mbB
Schweigerstraße 2
81541 München
Germany
Community Plant Variety Office ‘CPVO’ or ‘Party Opposing the Objection’
3 Boulevard Maréchal Foch
49000 Angers
France
On 16 May 2022 the Appellant in Case A014/2020 lodged an objection (hereinafter “Objection”) pursuant to Article
48 of Regulation (EC) No 2100/94 of 27 July 1994 on Community plant variety rights (OJ 1994 L 227, p. 1)
(hereinafter “Basic Regulation” or “BR”) before the Registry of the Board of Appeal of the Community Plant Variety
Office (hereinafter “Registry”).
The CPVO Board of Appeal, composed of Mr Marcus Navin-Jones as Alternate Chairperson, Mr Hidde Koenraad as
the Legally Qualified Member; and Professor Dr Dirk Reheul as the Technically Qualified Member, gives the following
Decision: The Objection is dismissed.
I. Form of action sought
1. The Appellant requests the CPVO Board of Appeal in its alternate composition and convened for the purposes of
assessing the admissibility and merits of the Objection, including the action to be taken concerning the Objection
(hereinafter “Alternate Board”), to remove the Chairperson from adjudicating in Case A014/2020. The CPVO
requests the Alternate Board to dismiss the Objection, or consider it as inadmissible, and not to remove the
Chairperson.
II. Summary of the facts
2. On 19 October 2020, the CPVO adopted a decision maintaining the refusal of the application for a Community
Plant Variety Right in relation to Application 2009/0954 ‘Braeburn 78’ (hereinafter “Contested Decision”).
3. On 17 December 2020, the Appellant lodged an appeal before the CPVO Board of Appeal concerning the
Contested Decision.
4. On 19 February 2021, the Appellant submitted to the Registry its Statement of Grounds.
5. On 12 March 2021, following its review of the case, the CPVO Rectification Committee decided not to rectify the
Contested Decision.

6. On 22 April 2021, the appeal case was remitted to the CPVO Board of Appeal.
7. On 1 February 2022, the Registry sent the Appellant an email inviting the Appellant to indicate whether it would
like an oral hearing to be held and proposing the date of 25 March 2022. On the same date, i.e. 1 February 2022,
the Appellant sent the Registry an email indicating that it did want an oral hearing to be held, but proposing the
oral hearing take place in May 2022.
8. On 4 February 2022, the Registry sent the Appellant an email proposing the oral hearing be held on 17 May 2022.
On the same date, i.e. 9 February 2022, the Appellant sent the Registry an email confirming its availability to attend
an oral hearing on the proposed date. On the same date, the Registry sent the Appellant a second email confirming
the date of the oral hearing as 17 May 2022.
9. On 15 April 2022, the CPVO Board of Appeal served on the parties a summons to attend the oral hearing to be
held by video conference (hereinafter “Oral Hearing”). The date and time of the Oral Hearing was set at 17 May
2022 at 9.30 a.m.. The parties were informed, amongst other things, that a ‘dry run’ would be held on Monday 16
May 2022 at 9.00 a.m., to ensure the videoconference line and facilities functioned as required, before the Oral
Hearing. The parties were also invited, amongst other things, to provide pleading notes to the Board of Appeal
before 13 May 2022.
10. On 29 April 2022, an internal email was sent by the Technically Qualified Member of the CPVO Board of Appeal
to the Registry, copying others, stating “The BOA in case A014/2020 (Braeburn 78) wants to submit a number of
questions addressed to the CPVO Office and the Examination Office to be dealt with during the hearing of 17 May
2022. You can find the questions in the attachment. Can you provide our questions to these parties? Can you
confirm the reception of these questions ? Best regards [sender name and contact details]”.
11. On 2 May 2022, the Registry sent the CPVO and the relevant examination office (GEVES/INRAE) an email with
an attachment containing a number of technical questions (hereinafter “Board’s Technical Questions” or “BTQs”)
and stating that the Board’s Technical Questions were “to be dealt with during the oral hearing of 17 May 2022”.
12. On 13 May 2022, the Appellant sent the Registry an email informing the Board of Appeal that the Appellant was
“considering” whether it attended the Oral Hearing or not. On the same date, the Registry sent an email to the
Appellant requesting clarification on the Appellant’s communication. The Appellant subsequently sent the Registry
a second email at 16.10 with a letter attached. The email stated, amongst other things, “Please immediately pass
on this letter to the Board, there is no need for a dry run [to ensure the videoconference line and facilities functioned
properly] on Monday morning”. The attached letter stated, amongst other things, that the Appellant “will not attend
the oral proceedings and withdraws the request for oral proceedings” and set out a number of pleas and arguments
concerning Case A014/2020 (hereinafter “Appellant Letter of 13 May 2022”).
13. On the same date, i.e. 13 May 2022, the Registry sent the CPVO an email informing the CPVO that the Appellant
no longer wished to have an Oral Hearing, and providing the CPVO a copy of the Appellant Letter of 13 May 2022.
14. On the same date, i.e. 13 May 2022, at 17.59, the CPVO sent the Registry an email attaching 4 documents,
specifically: (1) 1 document containing written answers to the Board’s Technical Questions Document with 2
documents affixed as annexes (“CPVO’s Response to the BTQs”); and (2) a document entitled ‘CPVO Pleading
Notes’.
15. On 16 May 2022, the Registry sent the CPVO an email setting the deadline for the CPVO to provide comments
on the Appellant Letter of 13 May 2022.
16. On the same date, i.e. 16 May 2022 at 12.31, the Registry sent the Appellant an email stating “[f]or the sake of
completeness, the Board would like to share with you the CPVO answers to the Board’s questions prior to the oral
hearing”, and attaching the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs.
17. On the same date, i.e. 16 May 2022, the Appellant sent an email to the Registry, and to the CPVO, enclosing 1
attachment. The attachment was a letter addressed to the Chairperson of the CPVO Board of Appeal and raising an
objection pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation (hereinafter “Objection Letter”).
2 / 13

18. On 17 May 2022, the Registry sent the Appellant an email: (1) stating that “…[o]nly through your letter [i.e. the
Appellant’s Objection Letter], the Board became aware of the fact that this document [i.e. the Board’s Technical
Questions] was not sent to you before. This has clearly been caused by a human error for which the Board
apologises”; (2) inviting the Appellant to provide observations on the Board’s Technical Questions and the CPVO’s
Response to the BTQs within 3 months; and (3) stating that, by raising an objection pursuant to Article 48(3) of the
Basic Regulation there may be “a serious delay in the current proceedings” and requesting confirmation from the
Appellant that the Appellant wished to continue to raise the Objection. On the same date, the Appellant sent the
Registry an email stating that the objection it had raised pursuant to Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation remained
“unchanged” and that the Appellant would “try to accommodate the 3-month time limit”.
19. On the same date, i.e. 17 May 2022, the Appellant submitted to the CPVO a request for public access to
documents concerning the case-file in Case A014/2020.
20. On 25 May 2022, the Registry sent the parties in the appeal proceedings an email concerning the most recent
procedural developments and next steps in the main proceedings regarding Case A014/2020. The email informed
the parties, amongst other things, that the Board of Appeal had: (1) provided the Appellant the Board’s Technical
Questions and the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs and invited the Appellant to provide observations on those
documents; and (2) resolved not to include the document entitled ‘CPVO Pleading Notes’ and received by the
Registry from the CPVO on 16 May 2022, in the appeal case file, and that the document would not be considered
by the Board of Appeal, as no oral hearing was currently scheduled.
21. On 2 June 2022, the CPVO sent the Registry an email requesting a time extension for the CPVO to provide
observations on the Appellant Letter of 13 May 2022.
22. On 7 June 2022, the Registry sent the CPVO an email informing the CPVO that a time extension to provide
observations on the Appellant Letter of 13 May 2022 was granted.
23. On 8 June 2022, the Registry sent the Appellant documents concerning the case-file in Case A014/2020.
24. On 18 July 2022, the CPVO sent the Registry an email with a document attached. The attached document
contained the CPVO’s observations on the Appellant Letter of 13 May 2022.
25. On 10 August 2022, the Appellant sent the Registry an email with a letter attached, requesting a time extension
to the deadline for the Appellant to provide observations on the Board’s Technical Questions and the CPVO’s
Response to the BTQs.
26. On 11 August 2022, the Registry sent the Appellant an email informing the Appellant that the deadline for the
Appellant to provide observations on the Board’s Technical Questions and the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, had
been extended.
27. On 26 August 2022, the Appellant sent the Registry an email with a document attached. The document contained
the Appellant’s observations on the Board’s Technical Questions and the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs.
III. Procedure following the lodgement of the Objection
28. As stated at paragraph 17 above, on 16 May 2022 the Appellant lodged, with the Registry, an objection pursuant
to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation, by way of a letter. The Objection was directed at the Chairperson of the CPVO
Board of Appeal.
29. On 20 May 2022, the Board of Appeal resolved to convene a panel of members to examine the Objection
comprising Mr Marcus Navin-Jones as Alternate Chairperson, Mr Hidde Koenraad as the Legally Qualified Member;
and Professor Dr Dirk Reheul as the Technically Qualified Member.
30. On 25 May 2022, the Registry sent the parties in the appeal proceedings an email concerning the Objection with
an attachment. The email and attachment: (1) informed the parties that an Article 48 BR Objection had been lodged;
(2) set out the action the Alternate Board intended to take following the lodgement of the Objection; and (3) set
out a number of questions addressed to each party concerning the Objection (hereinafter “Alternate Board’s
Questions”).
3 / 13

31. On 28 June 2022, the Appellant provided the Registry its reply to the Alternate Board’s Questions.
32. On 30 June 2022, the CPVO provided the Registry its reply to the Alternate Board’s Questions.
33. On 6 July 2022, the Alternate Board invited each party to provide its observations on the other party’s replies to
the Alternate Board’s Questions, and to provide any other comments as necessary. The Alternate Board also invited
the parties to indicate whether they wished to hold a virtual (on line) meeting to provide oral submissions in relation
to the Objection.
34. On 5 August 2022, the CPVO provided the Registry its observations on the replies and informed the Registry
that the CPVO did not request an oral hearing regarding the Objection.
35. On 26 August 2022, the Appellant provided the Registry its observations on the replies.
36. On 2 September 2022, the Registry sent the Appellant an email giving the Appellant more time to indicate
whether the Appellant requested a virtual (on line) meeting to provide oral submissions regarding the Objection.
37. On 7 September 2022, the Appellant sent the Registry an email with a letter attached, informing the Registry
that the Appellant did not request an oral hearing regarding the Objection.
38. On 14 September 2022, as none of the parties requested an online (virtual) oral hearing concerning the
Objection, and as the Alternate Board considered it had sufficient information to decide on the Objection, the parties
were informed that no online (virtual) oral hearing concerning the Objection would be convened, and that the
Alternate Board would proceed with issuing a Decision concerning the Objection in due course.
IV. Admissibility
39. The Appellant asserts that the Objection is admissible. The Appellant submits that no procedural step has been
taken rendering the Objection inadmissible pursuant to Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation. According to the
Appellant, the statements contained within its Objection Letter calling upon the CPVO Board of Appeal to “grant
[the Appellant] a sufficient written submission period” to provide written observations on the Board’s Technical
Questions and the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs did not “constitute a request or opinion within the meaning of the
second sentence of Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation”. The Appellant asserts that these statements were “merely
an indication that the Board of Appeal must give the Appellant an opportunity to comment on the questions raised
by the Board of Appeal and the CPVO’s replies”.
40. The CPVO takes the view that the Objection should be regarded as inadmissible. That is because, according to
the CPVO, a procedural step has been taken which renders the Objection as inadmissible. In the CPVO’s view,
according to a literal and teleological interpretation of Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation, the term “procedural
step” should be interpreted in a broad manner to include, amongst other things, “the appellant’s submission of
observations to the CPVO’s answers to the Board’s Technical Questions” and, in addition, “a…step as that in the
present case, namely, a step based on which the concerned party is afforded of a sort of “remedy” for the action or
reason that raised his/her concern of partiality”.
Findings of the Board
41. Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation states:
Members of the Boards of Appeal may be objected to by any party to the appeal proceedings for one of
the reasons mentioned in paragraph 1, or if suspected of partiality. An objection shall not be admissible if,
while being aware of a reason for objecting, the party to the appeal proceedings has taken a procedural
step. No objection may be based on the nationality of members.
42. It is the Appellant, who is a party to the appeal proceedings, who has raised an objection under Article 48(3) of
the Basic Regulation in this case.
43. As the Appellant clarified in its reply to the Alternate Board’s Questions, the Objection has been raised against
the Chairperson, and the Chairperson alone, who is a member of the CPVO Board of Appeal.
4 / 13

44. The reason for the Objection concerns a suspicion of partiality. As the Appellant clarified in its reply to the
Alternate Board’s Questions, the Appellant has not raised the Objection for any of the reasons set out in paragraph
1 of Article 48 of the Basic Regulation, or for any other reason. The Alternate Board therefore concludes that it is
the time at which the Appellant became aware of the suspicion of partiality, and whether or not the Appellant took
a procedural step prior to this point, which is of primary legal importance. In this regard the Alternate Board notes
that the Boards of Appeal of the European Patent Office (hereinafter “EPO”) have concluded that, in a situation
where a party had raised a partiality objection before the EPO Boards of Appeal and then, subsequently, lodged
certain new requests after the objection proceedings under Article 24(4) of the European Patent Convention 1973
had commenced – those requests did not render the partiality objection inadmissible (See Case T 1020/06 of 15
May 2009 ECLI:EP:BA:2009:T102006.20090515).
45. The suspicion of partiality in this case is based on the events concerning the Board’s Technical Questions and
the Oral Hearing, and the subsequent and related issues. The Appellant became aware of the Board’s Technical
Questions on 16 May 2022. The Appellant raised the Objection on the same day, i.e. 16 May 2022.
46. The Alternate Board notes that the Appellant raised the Objection by way of the Objection Letter which consisted
of 2 parts: the first part containing the Objection itself, the second and subsequent part setting out certain points
regarding the future conduct of the appeal proceedings. Although comprising of 2 parts, the Board of Appeal
considers that the underlying intention and purpose of the Objection Letter was clear – namely to raise an objection
pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation. Moreover, the Alternate Board finds that at the time the Appellant
became aware of the suspicion of partiality, the Appellant had not taken a relevant procedural step. As such, the
Alternate Board finds that the conditions concerning admissibility were, in this regard, met. Developments in the
appeal case following the submission of the Objection to the CPVO Board of Appeal, including the Appellant’s
responses to requests and invitations from the CPVO Board of Appeal, do not call into question this finding, nor the
admissibility of the Objection in this case.
47. The Alternate Board therefore concludes the Objection is admissible.
V. Substance
48. In support of the Objection, the Appellant relies on the following pleas and arguments:
(1) the Appellant rejects the Chairperson pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation;
(2) as it has a suspicion of partiality regarding the Chairperson which is reasonable given the facts, the
Chairperson must be removed; and
(3) even if the alleged infringement of the procedural rules are rectified, the Chairperson must still be removed,
as, following the conduct of the appeal proceedings to-date, the Appellant cannot expect a fair trial under
the Chairperson, and the Appellant’s suspicion of partiality would, in any event, continue to persist.
First Plea: Appellant’s purported rejection of the Chairperson pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic
Regulation
49. The Appellant clarified in its Reply to the Alternate Board’s Questions, that, according to its reading of Article
48(3) of the Basic Regulation, “members of the Boards of Appeal may be rejected by any party to the appeal
proceedings on the basis of a suspicion of partiality”. According to the Appellant, if there is a relevant suspicion of
partiality “the legal consequence of Article 48(1) of the Basic Regulation shall apply [i.e.] ‘The members of the
Boards of Appeal shall not participate in appeal proceedings,...’.” The Appellant references the German version of
the legal text of Article 48 of the Basic Regulation, which states, in relevant part:
Artikel 48
Ausschließung und Ablehnung
[…]
(3) Die Mitglieder der Beschwerdekammern können von jedem Beteiligten am Beschwerdeverfahren aus
einem der in Absatz 1 genannten Gründe oder wegen Besorgnis der Befangenheit abgelehnt werden.
50. The CPVO rejects this plea and the related lines of argument.
5 / 13

Findings of the Board
51. By the Appellant’s first plea and related arguments, the Alternate Board understands that, according to the
Appellant, Article 48 of the Basic Regulation affords any party to appeal proceedings the right to reject a member
of the CPVO Board of Appeal if that party, amongst other things, has a relevant suspicion of partiality relating to the
member in question. According to the Appellant, as it has raised an objection regarding suspected partiality directed
at the Chairperson in this case satisfying the relevant legal criterion (i.e. the applicant has a relevant suspicion of
partiality), the Chairperson must be removed pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation.
52. The Alternate Board observes that the examination of the first plea requires the interpretation of Article 48(3)
of the Basic Regulation.
53. As a preliminary remark, the Alternate Board recalls that, in determining the scope of a provision of European
Union law, regard must, as a general rule, first be had to its wording (see, for example, Case T-521/14, Sweden v
Commission, EU:T:2015:976, paragraph 59; see also, to that effect, Case C-383/14, Sodiaal International,
EU:C:2015:541, paragraphs 20 and 24). Where, on the basis of the wording alone, the text is not, in itself,
sufficiently clear, regard must be had to the context and objectives of the provision in question (see, for example,
Case C-453/14, Vorarlberger Gebietskrankenkasse, EU:C:2016:37, paragraph 27 and the case-law cited; Case T-
521/14, Sweden v Commission, EU:T:2015:976, paragraph 57 and the case-law cited).
54. The Alternate Board also recalls that when assessing the wording of a provision of European Union law, it is
important to bear in mind that European Union legislation is drafted in several languages and that the different
language versions are all equally authentic. An interpretation of a provision of Community law thus involves a
comparison of the different language versions (see, for example, Case 283/81, Srl CILFIT and Lanificio di Gavardo
SpA v Ministry of Health, EU:C:1982:335, paragraph 18). The necessity for uniform application, and accordingly
interpretation, of European Union law makes it impossible to consider one version of the legal text in isolation but
requires that it be interpreted on the basis of, in particular, the different language versions (see, Case 29/69, Erich
Stauder v City of Ulm – Sozialamt, EU:C:1969:57, paragraph 3). Where there is a divergence between the various
language versions of the EU legislative text, the need for uniform interpretation and application requires that the
provision in question be interpreted by reference to the purpose and general scheme of the rules which it forms
part (see CPVO Board of Appeal Procedural Decision in Joined appeal cases A007/2009, A002/2010 and A003/2010,
Sumost 02, paragraph 44 and the case law cited therein).
55. In order to assess the wording of Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation, the Alternate Board therefore finds it
necessary to assess the German version of the legal text and, in addition, the other (non German) versions of the
legal text.
56. As regards the German version of the legal text, the Alternate Board observes, amongst other things, the use
of the terms “Ablehnung” and “abgelehnt” in Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation. The Alternate Board notes that,
given, in particular, the wording of the German legal text, it could be possible to interpret the German language
version of the legal text as affording parties to appeal proceedings with a right not to object to the adjudication of
a member of the CPVO Board of Appeal, but a right to reject to their adjudication. However, having regard to the
other non-German language texts of Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation, in particular the English, Polish, French,
Spanish and Italian versions, the Alternate Board notes that it is clear that Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation does
not afford parties to appeal proceedings with a right to reject to the adjudication of members of the CPVO Board of
Appeal, but a right to object to their adjudication. In accordance with the necessity for uniform application and
interpretation of European Union law, the Alternate Board finds that the German language version of Article 48 of
the Basic Regulation must be interpreted consistently with the other language versions of the legal text and, in
particular, as affording parties of appeal proceedings with a right to object, but not a right to reject, to the
adjudication of members of the CPVO Board of Appeal, where the relevant legal conditions are met.
57. To the extent there is a divergence of meaning between the German version and the other language versions
of Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation, the Alternate Board notes that Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation must be
interpreted by reference to the purpose and general scheme of the rules which it forms part. In this regard the
Alternate Board concludes that to interpret Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation as affording parties to an appeal
proceeding with a suspicion of partiality a right to remove or reject a member of the CPVO Board of Appeal from
acting on an appeal case – would be inconsistent with the scheme of procedural rules it forms part of. That is
because, as the CPVO Board of Appeal has already concluded previously: “…that interpretation would lead to a
situation where a mere claim of partiality against one or several members of the Board of Appeal would lead to their
6 / 13

substitution by alternate members. This would not only give the parties the possibility to modify the composition of
the Board of Appeal at their own will but would also make the first sentence of paragraph 4 of Article 48 devoid of
meaning” (see CPVO Board of Appeal Procedural Decision in Joined appeal cases A007/2009, A002/2010 and
A003/2010, Sumost 02, paragraph 45).
58. It follows from the above that, a party to an appeal proceeding has the right to raise an objection pursuant to
Article 48 of the Basic Regulation against a member of the CPVO Board of Appeal, but no right to reject a member
of the CPVO Board of Appeal from adjudication. As the CPVO has correctly stated in these proceedings, it is for the
CPVO Board of Appeal to determine whether an objection raised pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation is,
amongst other things, admissible and well founded and, in addition, and as stated in first sentence of Article 48(4)
of the Basic Regulation, “the action to be taken in the cases specified in paragraphs 2 and 3 [of Article 48 of the
Basic Regulation]…”. The Appellant’s purported rejection of the Chairperson in this case is therefore not well founded
and must be dismissed.
59. Given the above, the Alternate Board concludes that the Appellant’s first plea must be rejected.
Second Plea: Appellant’s assertion that it has a suspicion of partiality regarding the Chairperson
which is reasonable given the facts
60. The Appellant asserts that it has a suspicion of partiality regarding the Chairperson in this case which is
reasonable given the facts and, as such, the Chairperson must be removed from adjudicating in this case. In support
of its plea, the Appellant makes the following arguments.
1. The Appellant has a suspicion of partiality
61. According to the Appellant, the core question concerning the Appellant’s Objection raised pursuant to Article 48
of the Basic Regulation, is “whether there is a ‘suspicion of partiality’”. The Appellant states that, in this case, it is
the “person concerned” and only it could be expected to have a suspicion of partiality. The Appellant states that “it
is obvious that the CPVO assess the present situation, in which the allegation is that there is a bias in favour of the
CPVO and to the detriment of the Appellant, unlike the Appellant”. The Appellant states that the Appellant’s point
of view is therefore “relevant”, that the CPVO’s view “does not matter” and that “it is irrelevant whether the CPVO
considers that there is bias or not”. According to the Appellant, the Alternate Board must “assess whether the
applicant has a ‘suspicion of partiality’” which must be done “on the basis of the underlying facts”. This, according
to the Appellant, is “a legal decision” which the legally competent members of the Alternate Board must answer
independently. Whether there is a suspicion of partiality does not, according to the Appellant, concern whether there
are “serious doubts”. In the Appellant’s view “no actual partiality is required”. According to the Appellant, the
Alternate Board must therefore examine whether, from the Appellant’s point of view, following a reasonable
assessment of all the circumstances, there are doubts as to the impartiality and independence of the Chairperson.
62. The Appellant asserts that, in this case, it does have a suspicion of impartiality and that this suspicion is based
on a reasonable assessment of the underlying facts. According to the Appellant, a suspicion of partiality may arise
where “it can be concluded, from an objective point of view” that procedural errors are due to, or explained by, an
unjustified approach towards one of the parties, or an unjustified, targeted investigation into the collection of
evidence outside the formal proceedings and where the facts give the justified impression that there is partiality.
The Appellant states that it has a suspicion of partiality “on a reasonable basis” even if the Board of Appeal did not
wish to create that impression. The Appellant further states that its fear of the existence of partiality is “even
confirmed” by the “instructions” provided by the Technically Qualified Member of the Board of Appeal to the Registry
that the Board’s Technical Questions should not be “forwarded to the Appellant”.
2. The Appellant’s suspicion of partiality is reasonable given the facts and circumstances
63. The Appellant argues that it has a “valid” suspicion of partiality as the suspicion is based on the facts, which
include breaches of “fundamental procedural principles such as the right to be heard and a transparent and fair
trial”. According to the Appellant, the facts “allow it to be assumed” that the Appellant has a suspicion of partiality
which is reasonable. According to the Appellant, the supporting evidence includes the following:
(1) On 29 April 2022, the Technically Qualified Member of the Board sent an “instruction” to the Registry to send
certain technical questions to “only one party [in the appeal proceedings]”.
(2) On 2 May 2022, the Board of Appeal sent a list of questions to the CPVO and other parties, informing those
parties that the questions would be dealt with at the Oral Hearing (Board’s Technical Questions). The Board of
7 / 13

Appeal did not notify the Appellant “simultaneously”, but, instead only “after [the Appellant had] announced on 13
May 2022 that he would not attend the hearing”, “24 hours” before the hearing, and only “for completeness”.
(3) The Board of Appeal sent the Board’s Technical Questions to the “GEVES and INRAE examination offices” who
are two bodies which are not involved in the procedure “for no apparent reason”.
(4) The Board of Appeal failed to provide, and has not provided, reasons as to why the Board of Appeal did not
provide the Appellant the Board’s Technical Questions initially, and only after the Appellant had withdrawn its request
for an Oral Hearing.
(5) The list of questions sent by the Board of Appeal to the CPVO and other parties on 2 May 2022 are “detailed”,
“highly relevant” and “not easy to answer, extensive, complex and unanswerable without further factual
investigation”. By providing these questions to the CPVO and other parties it allowed the CPVO to be “better
prepared” and informed at the Oral Hearing than the Appellant. Moreover, the impression is that the Board of Appeal
wanted the CPVO to say certain things, and provide certain answers, at the Oral Hearing, i.e. “put [answers] into
the [CPVO’s] mouth”.
(6) The Board of Appeal excluded the Appellant from discussions between the Board of Appeal and the
CPVO/examination office concerning the appeal case “of highly relevant technical issues”, prior to the Oral Hearing.
According to the Appellant, “it was not planned” that the Appellant be involved in those discussions which is
“confirmed by the official file”, in particular the communication of 29 April 2022. As such, according to the Appellant,
the Oral Hearing was set to be held, and would have been held “taking into account information obtained in this
way”. The Appellant states that the Oral Hearing was therefore planned “to surprise the Appellant” on the
substantive issues and deprive the Appellant of the ability of effectively responding to them in an informed and
prepared manner. The Appellant submits that even if all the information and evidence had been fully disclosed
during the Oral Hearing, the Appellant could not have dealt with it in such a way as to ensure the equality of arms
between the parties due to the “scope and complexity of the information”.
(7) On 13 May 2022, the Board of Appeal received a written response from the CPVO to the Board’s Technical
Questions, but did not notify the Appellant “immediately on receipt”. The CPVO’s Response to the BTQs is a
document consisting of “10 pages plus attachments” and substantive technical submissions.
(8) The Board of Appeal provided the Appellant the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs “one day before the date of the
Oral Hearing, i.e. a date when the preparation of the oral proceedings by the Board of Appeal and the parties was
concluded and it was no longer possible to deal with the CPVO’s reply sufficiently in time” and only after the Appellant
had “withdrawn the request for the Oral Hearing”.
(9) Had the Appellant attended the Oral Hearing, the Appellant would have been at a “clear procedural
disadvantage” and there would not have been a fair trial.
(10) The Appellant has “serious doubts” whether the Board of Appeal would have sent the Appellant the CPVO’s
Response to the BTQs, had the Oral Hearing been held. As the Board of Appeal informed the Appellant of the CPVO’s
Response to the BTQs “for completeness”, the Appellant does not believe so.
(11) The Board of Appeal failed to provide the Appellant, and has not provided, the Board’s Technical Questions
and the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs ‘in the language of the proceedings’.
64. The Appellant also states that some of the alleged infringements of EU procedural law, and alleged actions and
inactions of the Board of Appeal, cannot be regarded as “human error”. As regards the Board of Appeal’s alleged
exclusion of the Appellant from the technical discussions before the Oral Hearing putting the CPVO in an alleged
better informed position than the Appellant, the Appellant states that this demonstrates an “obvious” violation of
EU legal principles concerning due process, and that it must be assumed that these events were not “coincidence
or an accident and not a human error”. The Appellant states that “There can be no mention of human error here”.
Instead, the Appellant argues, it must reasonably conclude these alleged actions and inactions by the Board of
Appeal, are due to a difference in treatment by the Board of Appeal where: “the CPVO is preferred and the
complainant is disadvantaged”. The Appellant states that the correspondence and documentation between the
relevant parties confirms the impression that “it was no coincidence or human error that the [Board’s Technical
Questions] were not sent to the Appellant”. According to the Appellant, the email of 29 April 2022 ‘instructs [the
Registry] to forward [the Board’s Technical Questions] to the CPVO and the Examination Body’ and asks the Registry
‘to confirm that the CPVO and the examining body have also received these questions’. According to the Appellant,
this is evidence that “it was…not planned to make the [Board’s Technical Questions] available to the Appellant” and
that it was planned that “[the Board’s Technical Questions] should be discussed directly in the oral hearing, without
the Appellant being given the opportunity to prepare well for it”.
65. The Appellant asserts that, given the evidence, the impression that emerges is that there is a “secret agreement”
between the Board of Appeal and the CPVO and that the Appellant has been a party in proceedings involving
“collusion” between the CPVO and the Board of Appeal. According to the Appellant, it was “precisely this impression”
8 / 13

and the “resulting loss of confidence in the impartiality of the institutions” which Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation
intended to counteract.
3. The Appellant has raised the objection against the relevant member of the CPVO Board of Appeal
66. The Appellant has raised the Objection against the Chairperson alone in this case. The Appellant asserts that it
is correct to raise the partiality objection against the Chairperson in this case as, amongst other things, the
Chairperson is “a legally qualified member of the Board of Appeal” who is responsible for ensuring that appeal
proceedings are carried out in accordance with the legal requirements concerning due process which include “the
right to a fair trial” and “the equality of arms of the parties”. In this case, the Appellant states that the Chairperson
“allowed or did not prevent” the Board of Appeal from discussing facts and asking questions before the Oral Hearing
with just one of the parties, and by doing so put just one of the parties in a position informed of the relevant
individual circumstances. The Appellant states that in this case, the Chairperson is responsible for ensuring situations
do not arise whereby one party is not informed of important issues before an Oral Hearing is scheduled to take
place, particularly where that situation is “not based on human error”. The Appellant submits that the Chairperson
“had the possibility at several times to ensure that the Appellant was also informed” of the issues to be discussed
at the Oral Hearing but “he did not do that”. According to the Appellant, the Chairperson would have allowed the
Appellant to participate in an oral hearing, while knowing that the Appellant was deprived of relevant information
“Colloquially speaking: the chairman would have let the Appellant run into the open knife.” The Appellant states
that it is “highly unlikely” that the Board’s Technical Questions would have been sent to the CPVO, and the CPVO
would have submitted its response, without the Chairperson’s knowledge as the Technically Qualified Member of
the Board of Appeal would have needed the Chairperson’s approval before taking action. Nonetheless, even if the
Chairperson did not know that the Board’s Technical Questions had been sent out to the CPVO and other parties,
and/or that the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs had been received by the Board of Appeal, the Chairperson could
and should have: found out that a matter of this gravity had occurred, informed the parties, and taken appropriate
measures, but the Chairperson “did not do that.”
67. The CPVO rejects this plea and the related lines of argument.
Findings of the Board
68. As a preliminary remark, and whilst remaining cognizant of the clear differences between the CPVO Board of
Appeal and the EU Courts of Law, and other Boards of Appeal, the Alternate Board recalls that Articles 6(1) of the
European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European
Union (CFR), are generally recognised as binding standards for proceedings before, for example, the EPO Boards of
Appeal (see, for example, Case T 1627/09 of 10 October 2013 ECLI:EP:BA:2013:T162709.20131010). As such,
there should be very strict observance of the requirement for impartiality (see Case Law of the EPO Boards of Appeal
Section III, Part J, Paragraph 1.2). The Alternate Board further notes that, when carrying out their duties, Boards
of Appeal should have regard to, amongst other provisions, Article 47 of the CFR, (see Judgment of the General
Court of 20 September 2019, Germany v European Chemicals Agency, T-755/17, EU:T:2019:647, paragraph 57)
including the general legal order.
69. Given the general legal order, the similarities which exist between the CPVO Board of Appeal and other Boards
of Appeal, and given the importance of maintaining the credibility and trust which exists between the CPVO Board
of Appeal and its stakeholders, the Alternate Board notes that observance of the requirement for impartiality by the
members of the CPVO Board of Appeal is of very high importance. As such, and consistent with the principle of
good administration which requires, amongst other things, that relevant bodies examine “carefully and impartially”
all the relevant facts of a case (Judgment of the General Court, 3 October 2019, BASF v European Chemicals Agency,
T-805/17, EU:T:2019:723, paragraph 57), and in line with Article 15(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the
European Union (“TFEU”) concerning openness and transparency in the work of EU agencies and bodies, the
Alternate Board finds that it is incumbent on the CPVO Board of Appeal to ensure, insofar as it is relevant to the
CPVO Board of Appeal affairs, that justice and adherence to the principle of good administration, are not merely
done, they are seen to be done.
70. As regards to objections brought by parties pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation, the Alternate Board
notes the following. First, members of the CPVO Board of Appeal are a priori presumed to be impartial. Second, the
burden-of-proof resides with those parties who raise an objection. Third, it is incumbent on those parties who raise
an objection to ensure that the objection itself is sufficiently reasoned and substantiated. In this regard the Alternate
Board notes that it is settled case-law that the facts must be capable of supporting and substantiating a suspicion
9 / 13

of partiality, in order for an objection concerning partiality to be upheld. If, for example, there are legitimate reasons
which validate the manner appeal proceedings have been conducted in the past, a party’s suspicion of partiality
based on the conduct of the appeal proceedings cannot be regarded as substantiated sufficiently or at all, and the
objection cannot be upheld (see to that effect CPVO Board of Appeal Procedural Decision of 15 May 2012, Ralf
Schräder v CPVO relating to Variety denomination Sumost 02, (“Sumost 02 Objection Decision”) (paragraphs 60-
67) and OHIM/EU IPO Boards of Appeal Cases T 0355/13 of 18 November 2015
(ECLI:EP:BA:2015:T035513.20151118) and T 1028/96 of 15 September 1999
(ECLI:EP:BA:1999:T102896.19990915).
71. The Alternate Board therefore finds it necessary to assess the evidence relied on by the Appellant to determine
whether, amongst other things, the facts are capable and sufficient to substantiate and support a reasonable
suspicion of partiality.
72. As regards the communication of 29 April 2022, the Alternate Board notes the following points.
73. First, the communication is not an instruction and does not contain an instruction. The communication is a
request to the Registry for certain action to be taken, without specifying how that action should be taken in practice.
More specifically, it is a request for the Registry to “provide [the Board’s Technical Questions] questions” to the
relevant parties. It therefore follows that the Appellant’s assertions that, for example, this communication: (1)
contained “instructions” that the Board’s Technical Questions should not be forwarded to the Appellant; and/or (2)
that the communication constituted an “instruction” to the Registry to send certain technical questions to “only one
party [in the appeal proceedings]” – cannot be sufficiently supported or substantiated by the facts.
74. Second, the communication does not mention the Appellant, and does not state whether the Board’s Technical
Questions should be provided to the Appellant or not. The email states that the Board of Appeal wishes to raise
certain questions to be “dealt with during the [Oral Hearing]”. It is sent in reply to the communication of 15 April
2022 containing the summons to the Oral Hearing, and which therefore includes the contact details of the parties
to the proceedings – including the Appellant’s. It therefore follows that the Appellant’s assertions that this
communication should be interpreted as a deliberate act intended to exclude or prevent the Appellant from receiving
the Board’s Technical Questions and, as meaning, for example, that: (1) the Board’s Technical Questions should not
be “forwarded to the Appellant”; (2) “it was…not planned to make the [Board’s Technical Questions] available to
the Appellant”; (3) this communication confirms that “it was not planned” for the Appellant to be included in the
discussions before the Oral Hearing; that it was planned that “[the Board’s Technical Questions] should be discussed
directly in the oral hearing, without the Appellant being given the opportunity to prepare well for it”; (4) that the
Chairperson purposefully “allowed or did not prevent” the Board of Appeal from discussing facts and asking
questions before the Oral Hearing with just one of the parties and by doing so intentionally put on of the parties in
a better informed position than the other; and/or (5) that the Chairperson intended that the Board’s Technical
Questions were communicated to certain parties in a non bona fide manner so as to assist the CPVO and the
Examination office to prepare for the Oral Hearing, and/or to “put [answers] into the [CPVO’s] mouth” and/or to
exclude the Appellant from preparing answers to these questions – cannot be sufficiently supported or substantiated
by the facts.
75. Third, the communication was sent by the Technically Qualified Member. It was not sent by the Chairperson,
nor was the communication sent in the name of the Chairperson or the members of the Board of Appeal. The
Alternate Board notes, in this regard, and amongst other things, the complimentary close, sender name, and
signature block contained within the email. Moreover, the Alternate Board also notes, in this regard, the legal and
factual context within which this communication was sent.
76. In appeal cases before the CPVO Board of Appeal, a chairperson is legally required to assign the examination of
the appeal to one of the members as rapporteur, which “may include, where appropriate, the taking of evidence”
(Article 11(3) of the Proceedings Regulation). A chairperson may, therefore, appoint a technically qualified member
of the CPVO Board of Appeal to act as rapporteur and assign examination to the technically qualified member.
However, in those cases where a technically qualified member wishes to obtain certain evidence, it is incumbent
upon the technically qualified member, the Registry, and other relevant individuals, to obtain the Chairperson’s
express authorisation, including any clarification of an instruction, before taking any relevant action to ensure,
amongst other things, EU law is strictly adhered to. In this case, the Alternate Board notes that there was no
authorisation or instruction from the Chairperson to exclude the Appellant in the communications concerning the
scheduled Oral Hearing, or for the Registry not to provide the Board’s Technical Questions to the Appellant, and
that no such authorisation or instruction can be inferred. The Alternate Board further notes that the evidence in this
10 / 13

regard, namely the absence of authorisation and instruction from the Chairperson, cannot be regarded as evidence
giving rise to a reasonable suspicion of partiality. Given these points, the Alternate Board finds that, contrary to the
Appellant’s assertions, the communication of 29 April 2022 cannot be regarded as giving rise to a reasonable
suspicion of partiality on the part of the Chairperson, and that any purported suspicion of partiality cannot be
sufficiently supported or substantiated by the underlying facts.
77. Given the above, the Alternate Board finds that, the communication of 29 April 2022, cannot and does not
substantiate or support, sufficiently or at all, a reasonable suspicion of partiality on the part of the Chairperson.
78. As regards the alleged exclusion of the Appellant from the communications between the Board of Appeal and
the CPVO/Examination Office before the Oral Hearing, the Alternate Board note the following points.
79. First, and as regards the Board’s Technical Questions, communicated by the Registry to the CPVO and other
parties on 2 May 2022, the Board of Appeal notes, as a preliminary remark, that the Board of Appeal has a right to
investigate the facts and circumstances surrounding an appeal “of its own motion” (see, amongst others, Aurora Srl
v CPVO (T-140/15) [2017], ECLI:EU:T:2017:830, paras 72-74, 77 and Article 51 of the Proceedings Regulation and
Article 76 of the Basic Regulation) which includes the ability to raise relevant technical questions before an oral
hearing with the parties. At the same time, and without it being necessary to rule on the alleged infringement of
the principles of due process or right to a fair trial, an issue which can only, in principle, be decided before the EU
Courts, the Alternate Board notes that the communication of such questions should not disregard or undermine the
rights of parties to an appeal proceedings, or put them at a procedural disadvantage. Where the Board of Appeal
communicates relevant technical questions to one party in the appeal proceedings and there is no valid justification
for an undue delay in communicating the same questions to the other party in the appeal proceedings which puts
one of the party’s in a potentially procedurally advantageous position; where the questions are not provided in the
relevant language; and/or where the questions are provided to parties who are not party to the appeal proceedings,
without the prior knowledge of a party to the appeal proceedings - there are, in principle, legitimate grounds for
raising an objection pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation which may be sufficient to substantiate and
support the objection itself.
80. Second, and as regards the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, the Alternate Board notes that this document was
submitted by the CPVO to the Board of Appeal unrequested and without warning, i.e. as a ‘spontaneous submission’.
Having received this document from the CPVO on Friday 13 May 2022 at 17.59, the Board of Appeal disclosed this
document to the Appellant on Monday 16 May 2022 at 12.31. The Board of Appeal therefore disclosed this document
to the Appellant within 1 working day of its receipt. It is incumbent on the Board of Appeal to ensure that documents
received from parties to an appeal are admissible, can be added to the case file, and take any further action
(including the redaction of relevant confidential information) before disclosure to the other parties to the appeal.
This is particularly relevant in light of spontaneous submissions from parties which are unrequested and unforeseen
(see to that effect CPVO Board of Appeal Procedural Decision of 15 May 2012, Ralf Schräder v CPVO relating to
Variety denomination Sumost 02, paragraphs 50-59). The Alternate Board notes that 1 working-day to review the
CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, particularly in light of its length and complexity, and then communicate that
submission to the Appellant cannot be regarded as inconsistent with the principle of sound administration. The
Alternate Board also notes that, by the time the Appellant received the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, the Appellant
had already withdrawn its request for an Oral Hearing, and prevented the Oral Hearing from going ahead in practice
by, amongst other things, cancelling the ‘dry run’ which was necessary to ensure the videoconference line and
facilities functioned as required, before the Oral Hearing. Therefore, the Appellant’s submissions concerning the
communication of the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs “one day before the date of the Oral Hearing” and the inability
for the Appellant to prepare answers to the Board’s Technical Questions before the Oral Hearing – are of no material
weight or relevance – as the Oral Hearing had already been cancelled, and the Appellant had already ensured the
Oral Hearing could not, in practice, go-ahead, before the Board of Appeal provided the Appellant the CPVO’s
Response to the BTQs.
81. Third, the Alternate Board notes that no Oral Hearing was held on 16 May 2022, and no oral hearing has been
held in the appeal proceedings. The Alternate Board further notes that had an oral hearing taken place, the Appellant
cannot know with certainty what would, or would not, have happened, and whether and how the alleged procedural
deficiencies, and concerns regarding a fair trial, would have been addressed. The Appellant’s assertions that, for
example, the Oral Hearing was set to be held, and would have been held, in a manner “to surprise the Appellant”
on the substantive issues and not in accordance with the right to a fair trial, or in accordance with the equality of
arms – are merely suppositions, and cannot be sufficiently supported or substantiated by the facts.
11 / 13

82. Fourth, on the 16 May 2022 the Appellant lodged its Objection with the CPVO Board of Appeal. On 17 May 2022,
the Registry sent an email to the Appellant stating “[O]nly through your letter, the Board became aware of the fact
that the [Board’s Technical Questions] was not sent to you before. This has clearly been caused by a human error
for which the Board apologizes”. That email also proposed immediate corrective action, in particular, it included an
invitation for the Appellant to provide written observations responding to the Board’s Technical Questions, and the
CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, within 3 months. The Alternate Board therefore notes that, having become aware
of the potential mistake in not informing the Appellant of the Board’s Technical Questions, the Chairperson, as well
as the other members of the Board of Appeal, took immediate, decisive and proportionate corrective action and did
so in a transparent and clear manner. Moreover, the Alternate Board notes that it can find no reason why this
proposed corrective action does not address or remedy the alleged procedural defects earlier in the appeal
proceedings and/or why this action does not redress any procedural advantage the CPVO may have had earlier in
the appeal proceedings. Lastly, in this regard, the Alternate Board notes that the corrective action proposed and
taken by the Chairperson, and other members of the Board of Appeal, was similar, if not the same, as the corrective
action the Appellant itself had suggested and described in its Objection Letter. It therefore follows that the Appellant
cannot now take the view, that the corrective action taken is not sufficient or adequate to remedy the potential
procedural irregularities that occurred earlier in the process – or that by taking this action the facts substantiate or
support the view that a reasonable suspicion of partiality concerning the Chairperson arises.
83. Fifth, the Alternate Board notes the practical and legal consequences following the cancellation of the Oral
Hearing. In particular the Alternate Board notes that the CPVO and the Examination Office had from 2 May 2022
until 17 May 2022 (i.e. approximately 15 calendar days), to prepare oral submissions concerning the Board’s
Technical Questions. In contrast, the Appellant has been given, in total, from 17 May 2022 until 31 August 2022
(i.e. approximately 107 calendar days), to provide written observations on the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, and
the Board’s Technical Questions, in part due to the language versions provided. The Alternate Board therefore
concludes that the Appellant has not been put at any procedural disadvantage as regards, for example, its ability to
effectively make known its views on the Board’s Technical Questions and/or the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, or
relating to the failure to notify the Appellant of the Board’s Technical Questions before the Oral Hearing scheduled
for 17 May 2022, which did not take place.
84. Given the above, the Alternate Board finds that, the events leading up to the Oral Hearing scheduled for 17 May
2022, when considered together and in particular in light of the corrective action taken by the Chairperson, and the
other members of the Board of Appeal, on 17 May 2022 and thereafter, cannot and do not substantiate or support,
sufficiently or at all, a reasonable suspicion of partiality on the part of the Chairperson.
85. In light of the above, the Alternate Board concludes that the Appellant’s second plea must therefore be
dismissed.
Third plea: According to the Appellant, even if the alleged infringement of the procedural rules are
rectified, the Chairperson must still be removed, as, following the conduct of the appeal proceedings
to-date, the Appellant cannot expect a fair trial under the Chairperson, and the Appellant’s suspicion
of partiality would continue to persist.
86. The Appellant asserts, that as the Appellant was, amongst other things, deprived of extensive and complex
information relevant to the appeal proceedings before the scheduled date of the Oral Hearing “the Appellant must
come to the conclusion that it cannot expect a fair trial under the Chairperson”. The Appellant states that, even if
the potential procedural flaws and deficiencies are addressed and rectified, it would not render the Objection itself
as null and void, as, “after all, even [if the infringement of the procedural rules are rectified] then the suspicion of
partiality persists”. The Appellant states that in order to ensure that the proceedings are conducted correctly in the
rule of law, the person responsible for complying with a rule of law procedure, “namely the chairperson of the Board
of Appeal” as a legally competent member “must therefore be removed”.
87. The CPVO rejects this plea and the related lines of argument.
Findings of the Board
88. The Alternate Board notes that where there are no facts or evidence which are capable of sufficiently
substantiating or supporting a reasonable suspicion of partiality, a partiality objection cannot be upheld. Merely
because a party in the appeal proceedings purports to have a suspicion of partiality, or purports to continue to have
a suspicion of partiality, does not mean that the necessary requirements, as set out in, amongst others, Article 48
12 / 13

of the Basic Regulation, are met. Moreover, and in any event, the Alternate Board notes that, according to the case-
law of the EPO Boards of Appeal, which may apply by analogy to the CPVO Board of Appeal, partiality objections
involving procedural deficiencies are generally only capable of supporting a decision to remove or reject a member
of the EPO Boards of Appeal, if they “result from…a preconceived attitude or deliberate intention” (See Case T
1257/14 of 5 February 2018, ECLI:EP:BA:2018:T125714.20180205). As the Alternate Board has already concluded,
the facts in this case are not capable of supporting or substantiating a reasonable suspicion of partiality. This is
particularly in light of the corrective action taken by the Board of Appeal on 17 May 2022 and thereafter, which the
Alternate Board considers transparent, decisive and proportionate. That action in particular, removes beyond doubt,
any possible suspicion of partiality vis-à-vis the Chairperson, in particular any possible suspicion that procedural
deficiencies were the result of a preconceived attitude or deliberate intention.
89. On the basis of the above, the Alternate Board concludes that the third plea is not well founded and must
therefore be dismissed.
VI. Decision as to the Action to be Taken:
90. The CPVO Board of Appeal, in its alternate composition, orders that:
- The Objection be dismissed.
- The Chairperson not be removed.
- In light of the Appellant’s withdrawal of its request for an oral hearing before being informed of all the necessary
facts and circumstances, the Alternate Board recommends that the parties in the appeal proceedings be invited to
attend an oral hearing, and an oral hearing be convened, should the parties and/or the Board of Appeal consider it
necessary. In the event an oral hearing is convened, the Alternate Board recommend that the parties be invited to
submit new pleading notes to assist the interpreters.
